newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Ukraine's new currency will not solve old problems.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ukraine's new currency will not solve old problems.

text.p: Ukraine, celebrating the debut of its new currency on Monday, cannot look to the hryvnya to solve its economic problems, economists say.
Inflation has been brought down to Western levels in recent months from hyperinflation after Ukraine's independence in 1991.
But the economy, less than half its size in 1990, according to official statistics, is not set to grow until next year.
Economic problems have forced the authorities to postpone repeatedly the launch of the long-promised hryvnya.
But conditions now seem as favourable as ever and the new currency has good chances of holding steady, economists add.
Inflation is down, the temporary karbovanets currency is steady and the central bank has built up large reserves.
"There is no reason for it to devalue, there are no monetary reasons," said Rafal Antczak of the Harvard Institute for International Development.
The hryvnya -- whose name is taken from money used during the Kiev Rus empire about 1,000 years ago -- will be introduced on September 2.
It will be worth 100,000 karbovanets, the unwieldy interim currency also known as coupons, which will be withdrawn by September 16, lopping five zeros off Ukraine's unwieldy prices.
"The karbovanets has been fairly stable for the last six months and inflation was 0.1 percent in June and July," said Boris Najman, economist with the Soros International Economic Advisory Group.

The karbovanets, buoyed by central bank intervention, was unchanged at 176,100 to the dollar on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange all last week, unaffected by the August 25 announcement of the new currency. It was steady at about 180,000 at street kiosks on Friday.
But the inflation outlook for the next few months is uncertain.

The government has forecast August inflation at 5-6 percent due to price hikes in utilities and gas that started on August 1. Many stores and markets have rushed to raise prices before the new money's introduction.
Najman predicted monthly inflation at 2.6 percent in September, but said October's could be higher, when a month-long price freeze due to start the day the hryvnya is introduced ends.
Central bank reserves total about $2 billion, enough to keep the hryvnya stable.
"Bank reserves equal the total value of the currency in circulation. The central bank can back each hryvnya with dollars," said Alexander Pivovarsky of the Harvard group.
According to Viktor Yushchenko, chairman of the National Bank of Ukraine, Ukrainian money supply is 370 trillion karbovanets -- equivalent to about $2.1 billion.

Some economists said plans to phase out the karbovanets entirely within two weeks may be ambitious, and could cause confusion in the economy. The authorities have said the transition period will be extended if necessary.
Economists said the change, despite the new name, is really just technical, as when Poland removed three zeros from the zloty.
But such a redenomination can also help fight inflation by changing the mentality of consumers, who once again operate with low-denomination notes and coins.
But the broader questions of what currency regime the National Bank will operate remain open.
Yushchenko has said Ukraine will maintain a free floating exchange rate, but has also raised the possibility of tying the hryvnya to a single foreign currency or a basket of currencies.
The final outcome will depend on talks with the International Monetary Fund, with which Ukraine is negotiating a $1.5 billion stabilisation fund to back the hryvnya.
IMF officials in Kiev would not comment.

"The stabilisation fund is purely psychological, because it would finance nothing. But if people know there is money available to support the currency they won't be so afraid of speculative movements," said the Harvard Institute's Antczak.
Yushchenko said the stabilisation fund would be necessary to tie the hryvnya to a single currency or basket.
The authorities may need some kind of external link to shield the hryvnya from the temptation of easy solutions to Ukraine's financial problems.

Underlining the difficulties Ukraine's economy faces, President Leonid Kuchma announced only days before the new money comes in that the government will postpone submitting its 1997 budget, due in mid-September, to parliament.
"There are a lot of problems. We have a deficit of 1,000 trillion karbovanets ($5.6 billion)," Kuchma said.
Like other former Soviet republics, Ukraine's economy is hamstrung by debt, and the government itself has run up unpaid wage bills of hundreds of millions of dollars.
"Everyone is happy about the hryvnya but they are forgetting about the arrears," said Antczak.
The government has managed to arrest the growth of its wage debt, calculated at $500-600 million, he said.
Economists fear Ukraine could print more money to pay off debts, action which in the past sent inflation soaring and slashed the value of the karbovanets.
"It will be a political decision. They will have to decide on the best course of action, whether to print money, default, borrow, use credits or to issue government debt," Antzcak said.
